text: Forest ecologists have long known that the roots of most trees are colonized by mycorrhizal fungi, which trade soil minerals for sugars produced by photosynthesis. More controversial is the claim that these fungal threads link neighboring trees into a shared network through which carbon passes from large, sunlit trees to shaded seedlings. Isotope-labeling experiments have indeed detected labeled carbon moving from one tree into another. Yet detecting transfer is not the same as demonstrating that it matters. In several studies the quantities involved were a small fraction of a seedling's carbon budget, and some of the labeled carbon may have traveled through the soil rather than through fungal threads at all. Moreover, the fungi themselves consume much of the carbon they receive, so a network might serve the fungus's interests more than any tree's. None of this shows that the network idea is wrong; it shows that the popular image of trees deliberately nurturing their offspring has outrun the evidence.

stem: The primary purpose of the passage is
options: to argue that mycorrhizal fungi harm the trees whose roots they colonize
to explain how isotope labeling reveals the structure of fungal networks
to suggest that a popular claim goes beyond what the evidence shows
to show that shaded seedlings depend chiefly on minerals from the soil
to defend the view that mature trees send carbon preferentially to their own offspring
explanation: The last sentence states the point: the network idea may be right, but the popular image 'has outrun the evidence', and the middle of the passage lists reasons the detected transfer may not matter. The most tempting wrong choice is the last one, which restates the very view the author questions. The first choice is too extreme, since the author says only that fungi may serve their own interests, not that they harm trees.

stem: According to the passage, which of the following give reason to doubt that the carbon transfer detected in labeling experiments is important to seedlings? Select all that apply.
options: The amounts transferred were small compared with a seedling's carbon budget.
Some of the labeled carbon may not have passed through fungal threads.
The fungi use up much of the carbon they receive.
explanation: All three appear after 'detecting transfer is not the same as demonstrating that it matters.' The small quantities limit the importance of the transfer, the soil route questions whether the network carried it at all, and the fungi's own consumption suggests the network may serve the fungus rather than the tree. Readers who stop at the first two miss that the third is introduced by 'Moreover', which adds another reason of the same kind.

text: In much Baroque music, the composer wrote out only a bass line, sometimes with small numerals beneath it, and left the harmonies above it to the keyboard player. This practice, known as basso continuo, assumed a performer trained to turn a skeletal notation into full chords at sight. Modern editions often print a realized keyboard part, written by the editor, so that players without that training can perform the music. Such editions are convenient, but they can mislead. A printed realization looks as authoritative as the composer's own notes, and players tend to reproduce it exactly. The result is a uniformity the original practice never had, for continuo players varied their chords to suit the hall, the singers and the mood of a particular performance. The notation was not incomplete; it was deliberately open.

stem: The author's attitude toward modern editions that print a realized keyboard part is best described as
options: unqualified approval of their usefulness
appreciation tempered by reservations
contempt for the editors who prepare them
indifference to whether they are accurate
puzzlement about why they are published
explanation: The author grants that the editions are 'convenient' and explains whom they help, but then says they 'can mislead' because players treat the editor's chords as fixed. That mix of approval and concern is appreciation with reservations. 'Unqualified approval' ignores the criticism, and 'contempt' is far stronger than anything in the passage; the author never attacks the editors themselves.

explanation: The last sentence rejects a view a reader might form (that the composer left the notation unfinished) and replaces it with the author's view that the openness was intended. text: In negotiation research, the first number placed on the table tends to exert a disproportionate pull on the final agreement, a phenomenon known as anchoring. Experiments in which participants bargain over the price of a used car or a starting salary consistently find that the side making the first offer ends closer to its preferred outcome. This finding seems to contradict familiar advice to let the other party speak first so as to learn what it is willing to accept. The contradiction is partly resolved by attending to information. When a negotiator knows little about the value of what is being traded, an opponent's opening figure can reveal useful facts, and waiting has merit. When both sides are well informed, however, the opening number mainly shapes perceptions rather than conveying facts, and making it first becomes an advantage.

stem: According to the passage, the advice to let the other party speak first is most reasonable when a negotiator
options: is bargaining over a starting salary rather than over a price
expects the other party's opening offer to be unreasonably extreme
has already made several concessions to the other side
lacks information about the value of what is being traded
wants to shape the other party's perception of value
explanation: The passage says that when a negotiator 'knows little about the value' of the item, the opponent's opening figure 'can reveal useful facts, and waiting has merit.' The last choice reverses the logic: shaping perceptions is the reason to make the first offer, not to wait. Salaries and prices are both mentioned only as experimental settings, so the first choice draws a distinction the passage never makes.

stem: The author mentions the used car and the starting salary primarily in order to
options: give examples of settings in which the effect was studied
contrast two settings in which anchoring works in opposite ways
suggest that anchoring occurs only in negotiations about money
identify cases in which waiting to make an offer is advantageous
show that laboratory findings fail to apply to real negotiations
explanation: The car and the salary appear in a sentence describing experiments that 'consistently find' the anchoring effect, so they illustrate where it has been observed. They are not contrasted, since both lead to the same result. The fourth choice is tempting because the passage later discusses when waiting helps, but that point depends on information, not on these examples.

text: Tardigrades, animals less than a millimeter long, can survive the loss of nearly all their body water, reviving when moistened after years in a dried state. For decades, biologists explained such survival in desiccation-tolerant organisms by the sugar trehalose, which in brine shrimp and some insects forms a glassy solid that holds cellular structures in place. Tardigrades posed a puzzle, since many species contain little or no trehalose. Researchers later identified a family of proteins unique to tardigrades that lack a fixed three-dimensional shape in solution. As cells dry, these proteins appear to form a glass-like matrix of their own, and when the genes for them were inserted into yeast and bacteria, those organisms became markedly more tolerant of drying. The finding suggests that evolution has arrived at the same physical solution, vitrification, by more than one chemical route.

stem: The passage suggests that tardigrades posed a puzzle because
options: they survive the loss of body water for far longer periods than brine shrimp do
an accepted explanation of desiccation tolerance did not seem to apply to them
their proteins lack a fixed three-dimensional shape in solution
trehalose turned out to damage the structures of their cells
yeast and bacteria could not be made more tolerant of drying
explanation: Biologists explained desiccation tolerance by trehalose, yet many tardigrades contain 'little or no trehalose', so the usual explanation did not fit them. The shapeless proteins are the later solution to the puzzle, not its cause, which makes the third choice a trap for readers who match words instead of logic. The passage never compares how long tardigrades and brine shrimp survive.

stem: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage? Select all that apply.
options: Trehalose is not the only substance that can help cells survive drying.
Organisms that lack trehalose cannot form glassy solids in their cells.
The tardigrade proteins can protect cells in organisms other than tardigrades.
explanation: The tardigrade proteins also form a glass-like matrix, so trehalose is not the only protective substance, and yeast and bacteria given the protein genes became more tolerant of drying. The second statement is contradicted: tardigrades lack trehalose yet their proteins form a glassy matrix, which is the point of 'more than one chemical route.'

text: When Japanese woodblock prints reached Paris in quantity in the 1860s, they offered painters an alternative to conventions that had governed European picture-making since the Renaissance. The prints flattened space, cropped figures abruptly at the edges and set areas of unmodulated color against one another. Art historians once treated this encounter as a straightforward case of influence, as though French artists simply borrowed a set of devices. More recent accounts stress that the borrowing was selective. Painters took from the prints what served problems they were already pursuing, such as how to render the fleeting, partial views of modern city life, and ignored much else, including the prints' literary and theatrical subjects. On this view, the prints did not redirect French painting so much as lend authority to a direction it had begun to take.

stem: In the context in which it appears, “unmodulated” most nearly means
options: unvaried
uninterrupted
unpainted
unintended
unbalanced
explanation: The prints 'set areas of unmodulated color against one another', meaning flat areas of a single, even tone without shading or gradation, so 'unvaried' fits. 'Uninterrupted' is the main trap: it suggests unbroken extent, but modulation refers to changes in tone, not to breaks in an area.

stem: The more recent accounts described in the passage differ from earlier ones chiefly in
options: denying that French painters ever studied Japanese prints closely
dating the arrival of the Japanese prints in Paris several decades earlier
attributing the change in French painting to literary sources
arguing that Japanese printmakers imitated European conventions
stressing that French painters chose what suited their own aims
explanation: Earlier historians saw 'a straightforward case of influence'; recent accounts say the borrowing was 'selective', with painters taking what served problems they already had. The first choice goes too far, since selective borrowing still requires studying the prints. The passage gives only one date and never says historians disagree about it.

text: Economic historians have offered sharply different verdicts on the craft guilds of medieval European towns. One tradition treats them as cartels: by limiting the number of masters, fixing prices and barring outsiders, guilds enriched their members at the expense of consumers and slowed the spread of new techniques. A more sympathetic tradition argues that guilds solved a real problem. In markets where buyers could not easily judge the quality of cloth or metalwork before purchase, a guild's inspections and its stamp of approval assured customers that goods met a standard, and the threat of expulsion disciplined members who cut corners. The two views need not exclude each other. A guild could guarantee quality and restrict competition at once, and the balance between these functions probably shifted from town to town and century to century.

stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: explaining why medieval craft guilds eventually disappeared
presenting two assessments of guilds and suggesting that they can be reconciled
demonstrating that guilds raised prices far more than most historians have believed
describing the methods guilds used to inspect cloth and metalwork
arguing that guilds benefited consumers more than they benefited members
explanation: The passage sets out a critical view (guilds as cartels) and a sympathetic one (guilds as guarantors of quality), then says 'the two views need not exclude each other.' The inspections are a detail supporting one view, so the fourth choice is too narrow. The last choice takes the sympathetic side, but the author does not rank the two functions and says their balance varied.

options: Economic historians have offered sharply different verdicts on the craft guilds of medieval European towns.

The two views need not exclude each other.
A guild could guarantee quality and restrict competition at once, and the balance between these functions probably shifted from town to town and century to century.
explanation: The condition is that buyers 'could not easily judge the quality' of goods before buying, which the guild's inspections and stamp addressed. The sentence 'A more sympathetic tradition argues that guilds solved a real problem' is the trap: it announces that there was a problem but does not say what it was.

text: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it, which is one reason glaciers can persist in places where summer air temperatures rise above freezing. When the surface darkens, it absorbs more energy and melts faster. Soot from distant fires and industry has long been recognized as one darkening agent, but field studies on the Greenland ice sheet have drawn attention to another: pigmented algae that bloom on bare, wet ice during the melt season. The algae produce dark compounds that protect them from intense radiation, and in doing so they lower the reflectivity of the ice around them. Because more melting creates more of the wet surface the algae need, the process can feed on itself. Researchers caution, however, that the size of this effect varies widely between seasons and regions, and current climate models do not yet represent it.

stem: The passage implies which of the following about the algae it describes?
options: They darken the ice more than soot does everywhere on the Greenland ice sheet.
They produce dark compounds in order to warm the ice around them.
Their growth can be promoted by the melting they help to cause.
They grow most abundantly on fresh snow early in the season.
Their effect on melting has been measured precisely in every region.
explanation: The algae need wet ice, and their darkening causes more melting, which creates 'more of the wet surface the algae need', so they encourage their own growth. The second choice confuses effect with purpose: the compounds protect the algae from radiation, and the darkening is a side effect ('in doing so'). The first and last choices are contradicted by the researchers' caution that the effect varies and is not well represented.

stem: The final sentence of the passage functions primarily to
options: reject the claim that algae darken the surface of the ice
explain why soot is a more serious problem than algae
propose a method for measuring how much the algae darken ice
point out limits on what is currently known about the process
summarize the evidence showing that the process can feed on itself
explanation: Introduced by 'however', the final sentence warns that the effect's size varies and that models do not yet include it, which limits what can be claimed. It does not reject the darkening itself, which the researchers accept, and it proposes no method. The last choice describes the sentence before it, not the final one.

text: Many Victorian novels first reached readers not as books but in installments, issued monthly or weekly over a year or more. Critics have often treated this mode of publication as a commercial constraint that authors endured, blaming it for sprawling plots and contrived cliffhangers. Yet serialization also shaped the novels in ways that were not merely defects. Because readers lived with a story for many months, characters could age and change at something like the pace of ordinary life. Authors, moreover, could watch sales and letters from readers and adjust a plot while it was still unfinished, so that the novel became in part a conversation with its audience. To read such a work in a single volume, in a few sittings, is therefore to experience something its first readers never did.

stem: The author would most likely agree with which of the following statements about the critics mentioned in the passage?
options: They overlooked effects of serialization that were not shortcomings.
They were right that serialization had little effect on the novels' plots.
They exaggerated the commercial pressures that Victorian authors faced.
They preferred novels that were first published in a single volume.
They failed to notice that many novels were first issued in installments.
explanation: The critics blamed serialization for defects; the author replies that it 'also shaped the novels in ways that were not merely defects', implying the critics missed those positive effects. 'Not merely' concedes some defects, so the author does not accuse the critics of exaggerating commercial pressure. The second choice contradicts both the critics and the author, who agree that serialization affected plots.

stem: According to the passage, serialization made possible which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Readers could take in an entire novel in a few sittings.
Characters could change at a pace resembling that of ordinary life.
Authors could alter a plot in response to readers before finishing it.
explanation: The passage credits serialization with letting characters 'age and change at something like the pace of ordinary life' and with letting authors 'adjust a plot while it was still unfinished.' Reading a novel in a few sittings is what the single-volume reader does, the experience the author says the first readers 'never' had.

text: Creole languages arise when speakers of different languages, brought together under conditions such as plantation labor or long-distance trade, develop a shared means of communication that children then acquire as a first language. Because creoles form quickly, they have attracted linguists interested in how grammar emerges. One influential hypothesis held that creoles around the world share structural features, such as marking tense with separate particles rather than word endings, because children who acquire an unstable input fall back on an innate default grammar. Critics have replied that many of these shared features can be traced to the languages the original speakers brought with them, and that the similarities among creoles have been overstated by comparing only a few well-studied cases. The debate matters beyond creoles themselves, since it bears on how much of grammar is learned and how much is given.

stem: The critics mentioned in the passage would most likely agree that
options: creoles develop far more slowly than linguists once believed
children play no part in the formation of creole languages
creoles share no structural features with one another
tense particles are found more often in creoles than in any other group of languages
the grammar of a creole partly reflects the languages of its first speakers
explanation: The critics trace shared features 'to the languages the original speakers brought with them', so they hold that a creole's grammar partly reflects those languages. The third choice is too extreme: the critics say similarities have been 'overstated', not that none exist. Nothing in the passage questions the speed of creole formation or the role of children.

stem: Select the sentence that explains why creole languages are of particular interest to researchers studying how grammar arises.
options: Creole languages arise when speakers of different languages, brought together under conditions such as plantation labor or long-distance trade, develop a shared means of communication that children then acquire as a first language.

One influential hypothesis held that creoles around the world share structural features, such as marking tense with separate particles rather than word endings, because children who acquire an unstable input fall back on an innate default grammar.

Critics have replied that many of these shared features can be traced to the languages the original speakers brought with them, and that the similarities among creoles have been overstated by comparing only a few well-studied cases.
The debate matters beyond creoles themselves, since it bears on how much of grammar is learned and how much is given.
explanation: The second sentence gives the reason directly: creoles 'form quickly', so linguists can study grammar as it emerges. The last sentence is the trap; it explains why the debate about creoles matters to broader questions, not why creoles drew researchers in the first place.

text: Many migratory birds can orient using Earth's magnetic field, but how they sense it has long been uncertain. One proposal locates the sensor in tiny iron-oxide particles that would act like compass needles. Another, now favored by many researchers, holds that the sense depends on light-triggered chemical reactions in the eye. In this account, a protein called cryptochrome, when struck by blue light, forms pairs of molecules whose subsequent reactions depend subtly on the orientation of the magnetic field. Two observations support it. Caged robins orient correctly under blue or green light but become disoriented in red light, which does not activate cryptochrome. And weak radio-frequency noise, too feeble to move an iron particle but capable of disturbing the chemical reaction, disrupts their orientation. Neither observation proves the hypothesis, but together they are hard to explain by magnetic particles alone.

stem: The radio-frequency experiment is significant chiefly because the noise used in it
options: shows that robins can detect radio waves as well as magnetic fields
could disturb one proposed mechanism but not the other
proves that cryptochrome is located in the eyes of migratory birds
demonstrates that robins have no iron-oxide particles at all
makes robins disoriented only when they are kept under red light
explanation: The noise was 'too feeble to move an iron particle but capable of disturbing the chemical reaction', so its effect on orientation favors the chemical account over the particle account. The third choice overstates the result: the author says that 'neither observation proves the hypothesis.' The experiment says nothing about whether iron particles are present, only that they cannot explain this effect.

explanation: Only the last sentence weighs the evidence: it is not proof, yet it is hard to explain by the rival account. 'Two observations support it' is the tempting choice, but it merely announces that support exists without judging its strength; the sentence about the hypothesis being 'now favored' reports other researchers' opinion rather than the author's assessment.

text: The flying buttress is often presented as the engineering key to Gothic architecture: by carrying the outward thrust of a high vault across open air to a pier standing away from the wall, it allowed walls to be thinned and filled with glass. That account is correct as far as it goes, but it can suggest that builders first wanted luminous interiors and then invented a device to obtain them. The surviving evidence points to a messier process. Early buttresses were often added to existing churches whose walls had begun to lean, and only later were they planned from the start. Builders learned what the device could do partly by repairing failures. The soaring, glass-filled interior was thus as much a consequence of accumulated structural experience as the realization of a prior aesthetic program.

stem: The author's main objection to the usual account of the flying buttress is that it
options: exaggerates the part the buttress played in carrying the thrust of Gothic vaults
ignores the importance of stained glass in Gothic churches
implies a tidier sequence of goal and invention than the evidence shows
attributes the device to builders of a later century
treats the buttress as a decorative rather than a structural element
explanation: The author accepts the engineering account 'as far as it goes' but objects that it suggests builders first wanted bright interiors and then invented the device, whereas the evidence 'points to a messier process' of repair and learning. The first choice is the trap: the author never doubts that buttresses carried the vault's thrust, only the story of why they were developed.

stem: The author mentions churches “whose walls had begun to lean” most likely in order to
options: show that Gothic builders lacked basic engineering skill
explain why windows in later churches were made smaller
suggest that flying buttresses often failed to stop walls from moving
illustrate that buttresses were first used to correct existing problems
contrast early Gothic churches with the churches that preceded them
explanation: The leaning walls show that early buttresses were 'added to existing churches' as repairs and 'only later' planned from the start, which supports the author's account of learning by fixing failures. The third choice reverses the point: the passage implies the buttresses worked well enough that builders came to plan them. Nothing in the passage judges the builders unskilled.

text: Microfinance lenders in many developing economies have often lent to small groups of borrowers, each of whom is responsible in part for the others' loans. Such joint liability was thought to solve two problems that make lending to poor households costly: lenders cannot easily tell reliable borrowers from unreliable ones, and they cannot cheaply monitor how loans are used. Neighbors, by contrast, know one another's habits and can apply social pressure. Field experiments, however, have complicated this picture. In several programs, converting groups from joint to individual liability did not noticeably raise default rates, while it did attract more borrowers, some of whom had disliked being held responsible for others' debts. Regular group meetings, which continued under both arrangements, may have done more to sustain repayment than the shared obligation itself.

stem: The passage indicates that joint liability was expected to do which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Allow lenders to stop holding regular group meetings
Attract more borrowers than individual liability would
Let lenders benefit from what borrowers know about one another
explanation: Joint liability was meant to make use of the fact that neighbors 'know one another's habits and can apply social pressure', solving the lender's problems of selection and monitoring. Meetings 'continued under both arrangements', so ending them was never the aim. Attracting more borrowers is what individual liability did in the experiments, the opposite of the expectation.

stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the suggestion made in the final sentence of the passage?
options: Some borrowers left joint-liability groups because they disliked having to cover the debts of other members.
Default rates in the programs studied were higher in rural areas than in towns.
Lenders that adopted individual liability also raised their interest rates.
Most borrowers in the programs had known one another for many years.
In programs that stopped holding meetings, repayment fell even where joint liability was kept.
explanation: The final sentence suggests that meetings, not shared obligation, sustained repayment. If repayment fell when meetings stopped even though joint liability remained, the meetings would appear to be the active ingredient. The first choice repeats a fact already in the passage about why borrowers liked individual liability; it says nothing about what sustained repayment.

text: Reef-building corals depend on single-celled algae living in their tissues, which supply most of the coral's energy through photosynthesis. When water grows unusually warm, the partnership breaks down and the coral expels its algae, turning white, a process called bleaching. Bleached corals can recover if conditions improve, but repeated episodes often kill them. Some corals, however, host more than one type of alga, and certain types tolerate heat better than others. After a bleaching event, such corals sometimes recover with a larger share of the tolerant type, which makes them less likely to bleach in the next warm spell. This flexibility has encouraged hope that reefs might adapt to warming seas. The hope should be tempered: heat-tolerant algae often supply less energy, so corals that host them may grow more slowly, and not every coral species can take up new partners.

stem: According to the passage, a coral that recovers from bleaching with a larger share of heat-tolerant algae is likely to
options: stop depending on algae for most of its energy
lose the ability to host more than one type of alga
be less prone to bleaching during the next warm period
grow faster than corals that host other types of algae
pass the tolerant algae on to other coral species on its reef
explanation: The passage says the larger share of tolerant algae 'makes them less likely to bleach in the next warm spell.' The fourth choice reverses a detail: tolerant algae 'often supply less energy', so such corals may grow more slowly, not faster. Nothing suggests that the algae spread to other species; the passage notes that some species cannot take up new partners at all.

stem: The author's attitude toward the hope that reefs might adapt to warming seas is best described as
options: guarded
dismissive
enthusiastic
indifferent
bewildered
explanation: The author says the hope 'should be tempered' and gives two limits: slower growth and the fact that not every species can change partners. Tempering a hope is not rejecting it, so 'dismissive' is too strong; the author still presents the flexibility as real. 'Guarded' captures cautious, qualified support.

text: Scholars once assumed that a long poem could be composed only by an author who wrote it down or memorized a fixed text. Fieldwork among singers in the Balkans in the twentieth century challenged that assumption. The singers performed epics thousands of lines long without a written text, yet no two performances of the same song were identical. They worked with a stock of traditional phrases, each fitted to a particular place in the metrical line, along with familiar scenes such as arming for battle or a feast. Using these resources, a skilled singer recomposed the song as he performed it. Applied to ancient epics, this finding suggested that repeated epithets, long thought to be padding, were the working tools of composition. It also unsettled the very idea of an original version, since each performance was as authentic as any other.

signs of a single author's distinctive style
the most authentic parts of the original versions

explanation: The epithets were 'long thought to be padding', that is, filler that contributes little. The fieldwork recast them as 'working tools of composition.' The second choice is tempting because repetition can mark style, but the passage describes the epithets as shared traditional phrases, not one author's signature.

explanation: The assumption was that long poems need writing or a memorized fixed text. The third sentence reports singers performing very long epics with no written text and no fixed version, since performances differed. text: For a long time historians credited the printing press with transforming European intellectual life almost by itself: cheap, identical copies were said to have spread new ideas rapidly and fixed texts in stable form. More recent work has qualified both claims. Early printed books were often riddled with errors, and printers freely altered texts from one edition to the next, so print did not at once produce the stability attributed to it. Nor did manuscripts disappear; scribes continued to copy works for which demand was too small to justify a print run, and manuscript newsletters circulated alongside printed ones well into the eighteenth century. Revisionists do not deny that print mattered. They argue rather that its effects depended on the people who used it, and that they unfolded over generations rather than years.

stem: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: arguing that the printing press had little effect on European thought
explaining why scribes resisted the introduction of printing
describing how printers corrected the errors in early editions
comparing the cost of printed books with that of manuscripts
describing how historians have revised a once-dominant view
explanation: The passage outlines the older view of print as transformative 'almost by itself' and then the revisionist qualifications. The first choice is the trap: the revisionists 'do not deny that print mattered', they only slow and complicate its effects. Scribes are mentioned as continuing to work, not as resisting printing.

stem: Which of the following does the passage present as evidence against the claim that print quickly fixed texts in stable form? Select all that apply.
options: Scribes kept copying works for which demand was small.
Printers often altered texts from one edition to the next.
Revisionists accept that print mattered to European life.
explanation: The errors and the alterations between editions are given with the conclusion that 'print did not at once produce the stability attributed to it.' The scribes' copying answers a different claim, that print quickly replaced manuscripts, and the revisionists' acceptance that print mattered is a concession, not evidence about textual stability.

text: When the German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed in the early twentieth century that the continents had drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea. His evidence, which included the matching coastlines of Africa and South America and similar fossils on widely separated continents, was suggestive, but he could offer no plausible force strong enough to push continents through the solid ocean floor. The idea revived in the 1960s for reasons Wegener could not have anticipated. Surveys of the seafloor revealed stripes of rock magnetized in alternating directions, recording reversals of Earth's magnetic field, and the stripes formed mirror images on either side of mid-ocean ridges. The pattern made sense only if new crust formed at the ridges and spread outward. Continents, it turned out, did not plow through the ocean floor; they rode along with it.

stem: According to the passage, a major reason that geologists rejected Wegener's proposal was that
options: the coastlines of Africa and South America do not in fact match
he could not explain what force would move the continents
the fossils he cited had been wrongly identified
seafloor surveys had already contradicted his evidence
magnetic reversals had not yet been discovered by geologists
explanation: The passage calls his evidence 'suggestive' but says he 'could offer no plausible force strong enough' to move continents through the ocean floor. The last choice is true of the period but is not given as a reason for rejection; the stripes became important only later. The seafloor surveys came in the 1960s and supported the idea, so the fourth choice reverses their role.

stem: The final sentence of the passage serves mainly to
options: concede that Wegener's critics had been right about his evidence in every respect
introduce evidence that contradicts the account of seafloor spreading
explain why the magnetic stripes form mirror images of each other
suggest that the continents have now stopped moving
show how the new findings removed the objection Wegener faced
explanation: Wegener's problem was imagining continents pushed 'through the solid ocean floor'; the last sentence shows that, with seafloor spreading, continents need not plow through anything because they move with the floor. It grants the critics one point, that plowing was implausible, but not that they were right 'in every respect', since the continents did move. The mirror-image stripes are explained in the sentence before.

text: When photography became commercially available in the 1840s, many observers predicted the end of portrait painting. For the middle classes, at least, the prediction proved partly accurate: miniature painters, who had supplied small, affordable likenesses, lost much of their trade within a generation, and some of them became photographers or hand-colored photographic prints. Yet painted portraits of the wealthy did not decline, and in some respects their prestige rose. A photograph could record a face, but it could not easily flatter, and it was cheap enough that owning one no longer distinguished its owner. A commissioned painting, by contrast, signaled both expense and the attention of a named artist. Photography thus divided the market it had been expected to destroy, absorbing the modest likeness while leaving the luxury portrait more exclusive than before.

stem: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
options: A prediction is stated, partly confirmed, and then shown to be incomplete.
A theory is presented and then rejected on the basis of new evidence.
Two competing explanations are described, and one is shown to be superior.
A historical change is described, and its causes are said to be unknown.
A general claim is supported by a series of examples drawn from several different countries.
explanation: The passage opens with the prediction that photography would end portrait painting, says it 'proved partly accurate' for miniatures, then shows that it missed the rise in prestige of painted portraits for the wealthy. The second choice is too strong, since the prediction is only partly wrong, and the passage does give causes (flattery, cost, the artist's name), so the fourth choice fails.

stem: The passage suggests which of the following about photographs in the nineteenth century? Select all that apply.
options: They were less able than paintings to present a sitter flatteringly.
Their low cost reduced their value as a sign of social standing.
They took over much of the trade once served by miniature painters.
explanation: A photograph 'could not easily flatter', and it was 'cheap enough that owning one no longer distinguished its owner', which supports the first two. Miniature painters 'lost much of their trade' to photography, and the last sentence says photography absorbed 'the modest likeness', which supports the third. A reader looking for a single effect may stop too early; the passage names all three.

text: Economists have long argued that charging drivers a fee to enter crowded city centers at peak hours would reduce traffic more efficiently than building new roads. New roads, they note, tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it, whereas a price makes each driver weigh the delay his or her trip imposes on others. The few cities that have adopted such charges have generally seen traffic fall and travel times improve. Public opinion has followed a curious pattern in these places. Support is often weak before a charge is introduced and grows after residents have experienced its effects, a shift that suggests the main obstacle is not the policy's performance but the difficulty of imagining its benefits in advance.

stem: According to the passage, building new roads is often less effective than the economists' preferred policy because
options: new roads cost more to maintain over time than they cost to build
drivers generally prefer to use routes on which they are not charged any fee
the added capacity draws back drivers who had avoided the route
public opinion usually turns against road building over time
residents cannot imagine the benefits of new roads in advance
explanation: New roads 'tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it', so the gain in capacity is used up. The last choice borrows the passage's explanation for weak support for congestion charges and wrongly applies it to roads. Maintenance costs are never mentioned.

stem: Select the sentence that offers an interpretation of a change in residents' attitudes.
options: Economists have long argued that charging drivers a fee to enter crowded city centers at peak hours would reduce traffic more efficiently than building new roads.
New roads, they note, tend to fill up again as drivers who had avoided the congested route return to it, whereas a price makes each driver weigh the delay his or her trip imposes on others.
The few cities that have adopted such charges have generally seen traffic fall and travel times improve.
Public opinion has followed a curious pattern in these places.

Support is often weak before a charge is introduced and grows after residents have experienced its effects, a shift that suggests the main obstacle is not the policy's performance but the difficulty of imagining its benefits in advance.
explanation: The last sentence both describes the shift in support and interprets it ('a shift that suggests' the obstacle is imagining benefits in advance). The sentence 'Public opinion has followed a curious pattern' is the trap: it signals that a change occurred but neither describes it nor explains it.

text: Until the late 1970s, biologists assumed that nearly all life on Earth depended, directly or indirectly, on energy from sunlight. The discovery of dense animal communities around hydrothermal vents on the deep seafloor overturned that assumption. Far below the reach of light, giant tubeworms, clams and shrimp flourish around openings that release hot, mineral-laden water. The base of this food web consists of microbes that obtain energy by oxidizing hydrogen sulfide and other chemicals in the vent fluid, a process known as chemosynthesis. The tubeworms lack mouths and guts altogether; they house such microbes in a specialized organ and absorb the compounds the microbes produce. Even here, however, sunlight is not wholly absent from the story, since the oxygen many vent microbes use to oxidize sulfide is itself a product of photosynthesis at the surface.

stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the tubeworms described do which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: depend, at least indirectly, on chemicals in the vent fluid for nourishment
obtain nourishment without swallowing food in the usual way
live in a habitat that sunlight does not directly reach
explanation: The tubeworms absorb compounds made by microbes that draw energy from chemicals in the vent fluid, so they depend on those chemicals indirectly. Having no mouths or guts, they cannot swallow food, and the communities live 'far below the reach of light.' Each statement follows from a different sentence, so all three are supported.

stem: The last sentence of the passage functions primarily to
options: reject the claim that vent communities depend on chemosynthesis
explain how tubeworms absorb the compounds that microbes produce
argue that vent communities first formed near the ocean surface
qualify the extent to which vent life is independent of sunlight
show that the assumption held by biologists before the late 1970s was correct
explanation: After presenting vent life as running on chemical energy, the author adds that the oxygen many vent microbes use comes from photosynthesis, so the independence from sunlight is not complete. The last choice overstates this: the original assumption was 'overturned', and the final sentence only limits how far, rather than restoring the old view.

text: Translators of literature have long disagreed about how visible the foreignness of a text should be. One approach aims at a version that reads as though it had been written in the reader's language, smoothing away unfamiliar idioms, customs and rhythms. Its defenders argue that a translation should give readers the experience the original gave its first audience, who did not find their own language strange. Critics reply that this fluency comes at a cost: by making every foreign work sound familiar, it conceals what is distinctive about other cultures and quietly reinforces the reader's sense that his or her own conventions are natural. They favor translations that preserve some strangeness, even at the price of ease. Neither camp, it should be said, can claim complete fidelity, since every translation must choose which features of the original to sacrifice.

stem: The critics mentioned in the passage object to fluent translations chiefly because such translations
options: are harder for ordinary readers to enjoy
hide what is distinctive about foreign works
were never read by the original work's first audience
sacrifice fewer features of the original than other translations do
rely on idioms that most readers find unfamiliar
explanation: The critics say fluency 'conceals what is distinctive about other cultures' by making every work sound familiar. The last choice reverses the issue: fluent translations remove unfamiliar idioms rather than rely on them. Difficulty for readers is the cost the critics accept for their own preferred approach, not their complaint about fluent ones.

stem: The final sentence of the passage implies which of the following? Select all that apply.
options: Translations that preserve strangeness are more faithful than fluent ones.
Translators should stop debating how visible foreignness should be.
Every translation gives up some features of the original.
explanation: The sentence says every translation 'must choose which features of the original to sacrifice', so some loss is unavoidable. It denies complete fidelity to 'neither camp' and so does not rank one approach above the other, which rules out the statement that preserving strangeness is more faithful. Saying that both sides fall short is not the same as saying the debate should end.

text: A honeybee that finds a rich source of nectar returns to the hive and performs a movement known as the waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the run. The direction of the straight run, measured against the vertical surface of the comb, tells other bees the direction of the flowers relative to the sun. The length of the waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run, the farther away the food. Bees that follow the dancer then leave the hive and search in the indicated area. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a dancer adjusts the angle of its run over time, so that the information it gives remains accurate.

stem: According to the passage, the length of a bee's waggle run indicates
options: how far away the food source is
how much nectar the food source contains
where the sun is in the sky at that moment
how many bees should follow the dancer
how long the dancer spent searching for food
explanation: The passage states that 'the length of the waggle run indicates distance: the longer the run, the farther away the food.' The sun's position is tied to the direction of the run, not its length, so the third choice mixes up two different signals.

stem: The last sentence of the passage mainly explains
options: why bees prefer flowers that are close to the hive
how bees measure the distance to a food source
why some bees do not follow the dancer
how a dancer keeps its directions correct as the day passes
why bees dance on the vertical comb rather than outside the hive
explanation: Because the direction is given relative to the sun, and the sun moves, the dancer 'adjusts the angle of its run over time' so that its directions stay accurate. Distance is explained in an earlier sentence, so the second choice describes the wrong part of the passage.

text: When employers in several countries changed their retirement savings plans so that new workers were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out, participation rose sharply, often from under half of new employees to well over three quarters. Since the workers remained free to leave the plan at no cost, standard economic models, which assume that people choose the option they prefer, predict little change. The gap between prediction and result has been attributed to several causes. Deciding how much to save is tedious, and many people postpone tedious decisions indefinitely. Some workers may also read the default as a recommendation from an employer who presumably knows more than they do. The same research, however, found a drawback: many automatically enrolled workers stayed at the low contribution rate the plan had set, saving less than they might have chosen on their own.

stem: The passage suggests that standard economic models predicted little change because they assume that
options: most workers already save more than they need for retirement
employers know more about saving than their workers do
people will pick the option they prefer whatever the default
workers dislike decisions about saving and tend to postpone them
automatic enrollment is costly for workers to reverse
explanation: The models 'assume that people choose the option they prefer', and since leaving the plan was free, the default should not have mattered. The fourth choice is one of the explanations offered for why the models failed, so it is the opposite of their assumption. The last choice contradicts the passage, which says workers could leave 'at no cost.'

stem: According to the passage, which of the following help explain why automatic enrollment raised participation? Select all that apply.
options: Automatically enrolled workers chose higher contribution rates.
People tend to put off decisions that they find tedious.
Workers may treat the default as advice from a better-informed employer.
explanation: The passage offers two causes: people postpone tedious decisions, and some read the default as a recommendation from an employer who 'presumably knows more.' The statement about higher contribution rates reverses the drawback the research found: enrolled workers tended to stay at the plan's low contribution rate.

text: Painters of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries returned again and again to ruined abbeys and broken columns, and the fashion is usually explained as nostalgia for a vanished past. That reading is not wrong, but it is incomplete. A ruin is not simply what remains of a building; it is a building in the act of becoming landscape, as ivy, weather and collapse dissolve the boundary between human design and natural process. Many of these painters were less interested in the past the ruin recalled than in this ongoing transformation, which allowed them to depict time itself rather than a moment in it. The ruin's appeal, on this account, lay not in what it had lost but in what it was still undergoing. Nostalgia looks backward; these canvases often seem instead to contemplate a process that has no end.

stem: The author's attitude toward the usual explanation of the fashion for ruins is best described as
options: dismissive, since it ignores the role of landscape in such paintings
approving, since it identifies the painters' central concern
skeptical, since it rests on a misreading of the painters' letters
ambivalent, since the author cannot decide whether nostalgia played a part
accepting but reserved, regarding it as partial rather than mistaken
explanation: The author says the nostalgia reading 'is not wrong, but it is incomplete', then offers an additional interest in ongoing transformation. 'Dismissive' is the convincing trap, because the author does stress what the usual reading leaves out, but dismissing a view means rejecting it, which the author explicitly does not do. 'Ambivalent' fails because the author is decided: nostalgia played a part, just not the whole part.

stem: Select the sentence that defines the property of a ruin on which the author's alternative interpretation depends.
options: Painters of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries returned again and again to ruined abbeys and broken columns, and the fashion is usually explained as nostalgia for a vanished past.
That reading is not wrong, but it is incomplete.
A ruin is not simply what remains of a building; it is a building in the act of becoming landscape, as ivy, weather and collapse dissolve the boundary between human design and natural process.
Many of these painters were less interested in the past the ruin recalled than in this ongoing transformation, which allowed them to depict time itself rather than a moment in it.
The ruin's appeal, on this account, lay not in what it had lost but in what it was still undergoing.
Nostalgia looks backward; these canvases often seem instead to contemplate a process that has no end.
explanation: The third sentence defines the ruin as 'a building in the act of becoming landscape', a process in which nature gradually absorbs human design; everything after it builds on that definition. The next sentence refers back to 'this ongoing transformation' and the fifth restates the appeal 'on this account', so both depend on the definition rather than supply it. That dependence is the subtle trap at this level.
